newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Hebron deal in sight, Ross to brief Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Hebron deal in sight, Ross to brief Clinton.

text.p: Weeks of U.S. mediation between Israelis and Palestinians are finally showing results with a deal now in sight on Israel's withdrawal from Hebron.
U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross has headed home to brief President Bill Clinton on the talks which had been deadlocked since October. But he said he would be back next week to seal the agreement.

"I will be giving a positive report to President Clinton and I will be returning here no later than Monday, particularly because the work is going very well and because I hope and expect that we will conclude an agreement shortly thereafter," Ross told reporters after meeting Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Wednesday.
Negotiators were set to resume talks on Thursday in Ross's absence.

But as prospects for a deal grew, Israeli opposition to the withdrawal became more strident. Members of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's cabinet vowed to vote against the Hebron deal and settlers in the town clashed with Israeli troops.

Witnesses said police arrested about 20 settlers after an illegal pre-dawn attempt to take over two vacant houses in Hebron's Arab casbah. They said settlers hurled eggs, apples and stones at Israeli soldiers.
Hebron's Jews are angry about moves towards a long-overdue Israeli transfer to Arafat's Palestinian Authority of 80 percent of a town holy to both Moslems and Jews
At least four of 16 cabinet members in Netanyahu's government were expected to oppose the Hebron deal in solidarity with the settlers who say the agreement will leave them vulnerable to Arab attacks.
Ross said he was "very pleased with the progress that had been made" and was leaving members of his staff behind to continue mediation efforts.

"Both sides are approaching these negotiations as partners because their realise they're going to live together and they will create in this agreement and subsequent agreements a very real future...of partnership and reconciliation," Ross said.

Israeli negotiator Dan Shomron confirmed after the last round of talks on Wednesday that progress was made and his Palestinian counterpart Saeb Erekat said remaining gaps could be bridged within days.
"We had some progress in certain areas, we are trying to clear the text now to prepare the whole protocol but I would say there are still issues that we need to bridge," Erekat said.
"We still have some difficulties but we hope that in the near few days we will be able to conclude," he told Israel Radio.

Hebron, taken by Israel with the rest of the West Bank in the 1967 Middle East War, is the last Palestinian town due for self-rule under a 1995 peace deal. Israel's security fears have delayed its transfer.
Hebron's settlers feel betrayed by Netanyahu, who backs Jewish settlement in occupied lands but has promised to uphold the Hebron deal signed by the leftist government he ousted in May.
An Israeli rabbi accused Netanyahu of breaking a written election promise to the ultra-orthodox Habad movement never to cede land to the Arabs.
Ross's previous mediation effort, launched after a wave of clashes in the West Bank and Gaza in September, collapsed in late October with the U.S. envoy failing to broker a deal.
Clinton sent Ross back to region last Saturday after urging both sides to compromise.
